They look alike.
One stroke.
A whole new story.

日 and 目. 土 and 士. 未 and 末. If these kanji look like twins, you're in the right place. The trick is knowing where to look.

Let's spot the difference ↓

Reveal the answer: 未 or 末?

THREE PAIRS. EYES OPEN. 01 日 / 目 02 土 / 士 03 未 / 末 Little quiz ↗

Ever see a kanji and think, ‘I know this one’? Then you check the answer. Ah. That was its cousin.

It happens. When you're starting Japanese, an extra stroke or a slightly longer line is easy to miss. Here we'll put six easily confused kanji side by side. A few words, a closer look, and a little quiz at the end.

One thing before we start: a kanji can have more than one reading. That's why the pronunciations come with example words. You don't need to learn every reading today. Let's start with the differences.

01 /

COUNT THE LINES INSIDE

日 and 目: a day.
An eye. One extra line.

DAY · SUN

日

One line inside.

EYE

目

Two lines inside.

Count the lines inside, without counting the border.

The first pair slips in an extra line. 日 can mean sun or day. 目 means eye.

The simplest way to tell them apart? Look inside the rectangle. 日 has one horizontal line inside; 目 has two. Don't count the top or bottom edge: those belong to the border.

MEET THEM IN A WORD

日曜日にちようびnichiyōbi · Sunday

目めme · eye

THE MEMORY HOOK Think: ‘For eye, keep an eye on the two lines inside.’ It's a visual reminder, not an account of the kanji's origins.

02 /

FIND THE LONGER LINE

土 and 士: earth
has a wide base.

EARTH

土

Longer at the bottom.

IN ‘WARRIOR’

士

Longer at the top.

Same three strokes. A different line stretches out.

Counting won't help this time: both have three strokes. The difference is the length of the two horizontal lines.

In 土, earth, the longer line is underneath. Picture it as the ground beneath your feet. In 士, it's the other way round: the top line spreads out.

士 appears in 武士, ‘warrior’ or ‘samurai’, and in words for professions and qualifications. For now, we're mainly getting to know its shape.

MEET THEM IN A WORD

土つちtsuchi · earth

武士ぶしbushi · warrior, samurai

THE MEMORY HOOK Earth = a wide base. If you remember just one thing from this section, that'll do nicely.

DODON HAS SPOTTED SOMETHING

‘There it is.
That line thought it could fool us.’

Two pairs down. The last one has a familiar trick up its sleeve.Let's see what it's up to ↗
03 /

LOOK AT THE TOP TWO LINES

未 and 末: the future
isn't the end. Not yet.

NOT YET

未

Short above, long below.

END · TIP

末

Long above, short below.

Compare the two horizontal lines, from top to bottom.

Here they are: the pair from our opening trick. 未 means ‘not yet’; 末 means an end or a tip. Their two horizontal lines look as though they've swapped places.

In 未, the first line is shorter than the second. In 末, the first is longer. Focus on those two: the strokes reaching downwards won't settle this one.

MEET THEM IN A WORD

未来みらいmirai · future

週末しゅうまつshūmatsu · weekend

THE MEMORY HOOK The future is what hasn't arrived yet: 未来. For 末, picture a wide roof at the top: ‘This is the end.’ Two little reminders, not rules for every kanji.

YOUR POCKET REMINDER

Three differences.
That's it.

These diagrams compare shapes. They aren't handwriting models or stroke-order guides.

日 / 目
Count inside: one line / two lines.
土 / 士
Find the longer one: bottom / top.
未 / 末
Look at the first: shorter / longer than the second.

YOUR TURN

Getting the hang of a stroke.

Three questions. No timer. If you slip up, the explanation brings you straight back to the detail.

0 of 3 tried
QUESTION 01

Which kanji means ‘eye’?

Reveal the answer

目, eye. It has two horizontal lines inside.

QUESTION 02

The earth beneath your feet: which one?

Reveal the answer

土, earth. The bottom horizontal line is longer.

QUESTION 03

Complete ‘future’: □来.

Reveal the answer

未: 未来, mirai, means future.

AND TOMORROW?

You don't need to stare harder.

Try this: pick a pair, cover the explanation and point out the detail that changes. Then try recognising the kanji in one of the example words. Come back the next day and look again, before peeking at the answer.

Still mixing them up? Make the task smaller. For 土 and 士, just ask: ‘Which has the wider base?’ A specific difference gives you somewhere to start. ‘Kanji just won't stick’ gives you rather less to work with.

You don't have to conquer every kanji today. These six are a pretty good first meeting.

For your next step, there's a route through our practical guide to learning kanji. If you're still sorting out the writing systems, start with the differences between hiragana, katakana and kanji.

A COUPLE OF QUESTIONS? MAKE THAT THREE.

Before you go.

Do I need to know hiragana already?

Not to follow the visual comparisons. Each example has hiragana and a reading in Latin letters. Learning hiragana is an essential step towards reading Japanese, though: the romanisation here simply helps you get started.

Are all of these JLPT N5 kanji?

We chose these for their similar shapes, not from an N5 list. The kanji and words here shouldn't all be treated as material at the same level. You can understand the difference between two shapes without memorising every example right away.

What if I see them in another font?

The style can change: strokes may be thinner, slanted or more rounded. Look for the structure we've explored, such as internal lines and relative lengths, and compare the characters in the words as well as the diagrams. If a particular form is still unclear, the word and its context help you interpret it.

Behind the scenes: sources and notes

The structural differences in these pairs are also illustrated by Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs (Japanese PDF). For meanings and readings, we consulted KanjiPedia, the Japan Kanji Aptitude Testing Foundation's dictionary: 日, 目, 土, 士, 未 and 末.

The memory hooks and DoDon's remarks are editorial creations. The diagrams use Kanjidon's font to highlight differences; they don't teach stroke order. This article was created by the Kanjidon team.
